text:
Here's a little shop's orders table. Every row has a key, nothing's null... every constraint passes. But look closer. Ada's email is stored twice, and so is the notebook's price. So Ada changes her email, and a rushed update fixes only order one. Postgres says, update one. No complaints. Now Ada has two emails. No constraint broke... the design let one fact live in two places.

That's the update anomaly, and it has two siblings. Add a mug nobody's ordered yet? Refused, because every row here has to be an order. And when Grace cancels her only order, deleting it deletes Grace too.

The cure is one rule. Every fact gets exactly one home. Customers get a table, products get a table, and each order just points at both. Now Ada's email is one row to change, the mug can wait for its first order, and Grace outlives hers. Need the wide view back? A join rebuilds it, any time. Normal forms get you there in steps, starting with what fits in a cell.

First normal form means one value per cell. Here's Ada, with two phone numbers in one. Ask who has five five five, two thousand... and Postgres finds nobody. It's buried in a string. Phone one, two and three instead? That's a repeating group, with a ceiling. A fourth number won't fit.

The fix is a child table. Each number gets its own row, pointing back at its student. Now a search is a plain equals, Linus can have none at all, and a unique constraint stops Ada's number going in twice. So each cell holds one value. But what does each value depend on?
